summaryRaw: NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sent the following email to NVIDIA employees earlier today. I owe my family and all of you an apology.
I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.
To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

comments.author: Pentamerous
comments.textRawHtml:
Opinions on the affair and the public discourse aside, I have to say though that it is the first time in a long time that I see an apology letter written from a business person in the name of the company that actually admits wrongdoing and has accountability.

Usually they are more along the lines of fake apologies like "I'm sorry that you feel that way", or in this particular case I would imagine something like "I'm sorry that I was spied on, I was doing my best and nothing prepared me to deal with a foreign agent".

It's refreshing to see words like "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.".

children.author: nl
children.textRawHtml:
It's not exactly clear what (if any) confidential information he passed on was.

It's not exactly confidential that NVidia wants to sell more chips in China. They have publicly lobbied for it, and personally I think the evidence is that their arguments make a lot of sense.

The affair was dumb etc but from a business point of view it seems harmless.

From a geopolitical point of view one could me mischievous and argue that Jensen seduced a Chinese-linked tech executive and persuaded her to buy American tech instead of supporting domestic Chinese options. Good work Jensen!

children.author: arevno
children.textRawHtml:
In California, and most US states, divorce is statutorily no-fault.

Meaning that if she didn't like the stitching on Jensen's leather jacket one random morning, she could divorce him, and the courts wouldn't care.

Divorce is always a risk, whether your CEO is a Papal-certified Saint, or whether he drowns puppies in his spare time.

So sure, sell now, now that the risk of divorce is slightly elevated; but be not deceived: divorce is a risk at all times, for every corporate principal, in every publicly traded company.

We also don't know what private contracts, provisions, prenuptial agreements, etc apply. It's quite likely that they have a private set of agreements, if NVDA's attorneys are at all competent.
